## Why This Is Asked
This question tests practical knowledge of Kubernetes config management, deployment strategies, and zero-downtime rollouts. It covers ConfigMaps, envFrom behavior, and how to trigger updates in a safe way.

## Key Concepts
- ConfigMap-driven configuration without code changes
- envFrom and environment variable propagation
- RollingUpdate strategy with maxSurge and maxUnavailable
- Rollout triggering via template checksum annotation

## Code Example
```yaml
# ConfigMap example
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: feature-flags
  namespace: web
data:
  enableNewUI: "true"

# Deployment snippet (envFrom)
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web-app
  namespace: web
spec:
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 1
      maxUnavailable: 0
  template:
    metadata:
      annotations:
        checksum/config: "<hash-of-config>"
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: myapp:latest
        envFrom:
        - configMapRef:
            name: feature-flags
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you automate updating checksum/config when feature-flags changes?
- How would you adapt this approach for multiple namespaces with different flags?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests the ability to design safe, incremental releases using only Kubernetes primitives and a standard Ingress controller—no specialized CI/CD tooling required.

## Key Concepts
- **Canary rollout**: Two Deployments (v1 baseline, v2 canary) with two corresponding Services
- **Traffic routing**: Ingress canary-weight annotations control traffic split
- **Observability**: Readiness probes, Prometheus metrics, error rates, latency percentiles
- **Rollback**: Reduce canary weight to 0% or scale canary replicas to 0
- **Promotion**: Delete canary Deployment, update baseline to v2 image

## Rollback Criteria
- Error rate exceeds SLO threshold (e.g., >1% for 5 minutes)
- Latency p99 exceeds baseline by >50%
- 5xx error count spikes unexpectedly

## Code Example
```yaml
# api-v1 Deployment (baseline)
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: api-v1
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: api
      version: v1
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: api
        version: v1
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: myapp/api:v1
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 8080

---
# api-v2 Deployment (canary)
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: api-v2
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: api
      version: v2
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: api
        version: v2
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: myapp/api:v2
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 8080

---
# api-v1 Service (baseline)
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: api-v1
spec:
  selector:
    version: v1
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 8080

---
# api-v2 Service (canary)
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: api-canary
spec:
  selector:
    version: v2
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 8080

---
# Ingress with canary routing
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: api-ingress
  annotations:
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/canary: "true"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/canary-weight: "10"
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  rules:
  - host: api.example.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: api-canary
            port:
              number: 80
```

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

Tests understanding of basic multi-tenant isolation using Kubernetes primitives: per-namespace quotas, default resource boundaries, and scoped RBAC.

## Key Concepts
- Namespace-scoped quotas and limits
- Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) boundaries
- Validation of quota enforcement via kubectl checks

## Code Example
```yaml
# ResourceQuota (per-namespace cap)
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: team-a-quota
  namespace: team-a
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "2"
    requests.memory: 4Gi
    limits.cpu: "4"
    limits.memory: 8Gi
```

```yaml
# LimitRange (defaults for containers)
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: team-a-limits
  namespace: team-a
spec:
  limits:
  - max:
      cpu: "1"
    min:
      cpu: "100m"
    defaultRequest:
      cpu: "200m"
    default:
      cpu: "300m"
    type: Container
```

```yaml
# RBAC scoped to team-a
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: developer
  namespace: team-a
rules:
- apiGroups: ["apps"]
  resources: ["deployments", "statefulsets"]
  verbs: ["create", "get", "list", "watch", "update", "delete"]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: dev-binding
  namespace: team-a
subjects:
- kind: User
  name: alice
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
roleRef:
  kind: Role
  name: developer
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
```

## Follow-up Checks
- kubectl describe quota team-a-quota --namespace=team-a
- kubectl describe limitrange team-a-limits --namespace=team-a
- kubectl auth can-i create deploy --namespace=team-a --as alice
- Deploy a pod within quota, then attempt an over-quota deployment and confirm rejection.
